items.title: How to make faceless reels with Claude Code, in five steps
items.summary: How to make faceless reels with Claude Code, in five steps. One. Open my reel skill in Claude Code. Two. Tell it the topic and the reel you want to copy. Three. Give it one source file, because every number on screen has to be in it. Four. Let it work. It writes the script, records the voiceover, builds every scene, adds the captions, and checks each number against the source before I see it. Five. I watch it once, then post it. Then I make the next one. Idea: @adilet.fndr #shorts #claudecode #reels

items.title: Priya applied to 312 jobs and got three interviews
items.summary: Priya applied to 312 jobs and got three interviews. Mass applying with AI doesn't work. The fix is smaller: find the 15 roles where you're the obvious choice. Write one sentence: the kind of company, the kind of role, and the one skill you're best at. Hers was Senior PM roles at Series B or C B2B SaaS companies, where she can use her enterprise workflow expertise. Then you only apply where that sentence is true. Lower volume, higher success rate. Source: my Unicorn Candidate-Market Fit newsletter, Oct 31 2025. #shorts #pmjobs

items.title: Is AI Now Good Enough To Cure Cancer? | YC Paper Club
items.summary: This week’s Paper Club is all about AI for biology. The cost of sequencing has collapsed, which means biology now generates more data than anyone can mine, and the models are finally catching up. We cover how falling sequencing costs are turning cancer care into a per-patient data problem, what it takes to model a cell rather than a molecule, what a language model trained on DNA actually learns, and why in-context learning showed up in a genome model that nobody trained for it. items.title: How To Build The Future: Paul Graham & Amjad Masad
items.summary: Replit was building toward the AI coding era years before it had a name. In 2024, the company shipped an agent that could take a request in plain English, work through errors, provision its own infrastructure, and keep going until the software actually worked. The model companies even reached out to ask how Replit had pulled it off. Co-founder and CEO Amjad Masad had been thinking about making programming radically more accessible since 2008, and Replit’s original pitch deck predicted AI-generated code before the Transformer paper was published. Today, that same technology is moving into banks, manufacturers, and other large companies, where Amjad says teams are replacing software projects once scoped at $10 million with $250,000 of Replit. On How to Build the Future, Paul Graham sits down with Amjad to talk about why Replit was so well positioned when coding agents arrived, what comes after vibe coding, and his bigger vision for the “self-driving company,” where AI agents increasingly build and operate the software a company needs.
